Response-Time Equity and Demand Forecasting
in Chicago's 311 System

A 2019–2025 analysis of 4,286,964 service requests, 789 census tracts, and the long shadow of 1930s redlining maps
Prepared 09 October 2026 · Data: City of Chicago Data Portal, NOAA NCEI, US Census ACS 5-year 2023, University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab (HOLC) · Generated programmatically from the analysis pipeline

The headline finding is that raw 311 "response time" statistics for Chicago are not measuring what they appear to measure. 58.4% of all records in the dataset are opened and closed within one minute — citizen information calls and auto-closed noise reports that never involve dispatching a crew. Taken at face value they produce a citywide median resolution time of 0.00001 days (0.0 minutes), a number that says nothing about service delivery. Once those filings are separated out, the median time to resolve a genuine service request is 5.75 days, with a 90th percentile of 107 days.

Second, response times are not spatially random. Tract-level median resolution times show statistically significant spatial clustering (Moran's I = 0.5869; permutation p = 0.0010, z = 29.65, 789 tracts), and 118 tracts sit in significant high–high "slow" clusters — slow tracts are slow together, which points to a systemic geographic pattern rather than unrelated local problems.

A finding that did not hold is worth stating just as plainly. Requests in grade D ("redlined") tracts are not slower than in grade A tracts: the tract medians are 6.3 days for A against 5.53 for D (ratio 0.879×), and the one-sided test for "D is slower" returns p = 0.83. The expected 1930s redlining gradient is not present in 311 response time. With grade A containing only 6 tracts that comparison is weak in both directions, so it is reported as an unresolved null rather than as evidence of either equity or inequity.

What the tract-level regression does show is a race and income pattern rather than a redlining-map pattern: a one-point increase in a tract's non-white population share is associated with +0.0095 days to resolution (p = 0.064), and each additional $10,000 of median household income with -0.1436 days (p = 1e-06). The income term is the stronger of the two.

Third, demand is forecastable but seasonal naive is a hard baseline to beat. Across a 12-month hold-out the strongest model was SARIMAX + weather; weather covariates carry real signal for temperature-driven request types. Isolation Forest flagged 16 weeks as anomalous.

What this report does not claim. This is observational analysis of administrative data. It identifies where service is slow and that those places share a history of disinvestment. It does not measure crew routing, staffing allocations, or budget decisions, and it is not evidence that any City employee behaves differently by neighbourhood. The appropriate use is to prioritise audits, not to assign blame.

1. Business problem

Chicago's 311 system is the city's primary intake channel for non-emergency service requests — potholes, rodents, flooded basements, broken streetlights, tree emergencies. It is also the city's public record of how equitably it responds to its residents. Two operational questions follow:

  1. Equity. Does the time taken to close a request depend on where the request was made, after accounting for what was requested?
  2. Capacity. Can future demand be anticipated well enough to size crews and contact-centre capacity in advance?

Both questions are answerable from the public record, and both are easy to answer wrongly. The naive version of question one — average all closure times — returns a number dominated by administrative filings. The naive version of question two — fit a line through monthly totals — fails on a series with a hard summer peak. Most of the analytical work in this project went into avoiding those two mistakes.

3. Methodology

3.1 Geocoding to census tracts

The 311 dataset contains no census tract field — only community area, ward and coordinates. Tracts are therefore produced by a genuine point-in-polygon test (DuckDB's spatial extension, R-tree indexed) against the 2020 tract boundaries. 99.7% of rows received a tract; the remainder are records with no coordinates or points falling outside the city boundary, which are left unassigned rather than guessed.

3.2 The severity index

Raw resolution time is a poor proxy for service quality: a 30-day tree-trim is not comparable to a 30-day rodent complaint. Each request type is therefore classified into one of four severity bands — critical, high, medium, low — with weights 1.00 / 0.70 / 0.45 / 0.20, and a severity_weighted_days measure is reported alongside raw medians. The ruleset lives in a single place in the codebase and is loaded into the warehouse as data, so the SQL and the Python cannot disagree about what "critical" means.

3.3 The actionability filter

This is the methodological core of the project. 58.4% of records close in under one minute. They are flagged is_informationalis_actionable rather than deleted: volume and seasonality analysis keeps them, because a phone call is still load on the system, while every response-time statistic excludes them. The exclusion is deliberate and documented, not a silent filter.

3.4 Sampling design and its validation

The seven-year window contains 4.29M rows at full detail. To keep the pipeline reproducible in reasonable time, the earlier portion is a 20% systematic sample on the last digit of sr_number — a field assigned sequentially, so the sample is even in time — while the final 13 months are pulled at complete row-level detail for unbiased model evaluation.

This assumption was tested, not asserted. Exact full-population monthly counts were fetched from the API and compared against the sampled months: across 71 validated months the sample share averaged 20.002% (min 19.926%, max 20.129%). Weighting by 5 therefore reproduces true monthly totals, and the sample introduces no measurable time bias.

3.5 Analytical scope discipline

Two scopes are used throughout and never mixed. Demand scope (all rows) is used for volume, seasonality and forecasting. Service scope (is_actionable) is used for every response-time, equity and severity statistic. Any number in this report can be traced to one of the two.

Known limitations of the source data. Roughly 21% of records fall outside any HOLC assessment area, because the 1930s maps did not cover the whole city; redlining results therefore describe the mapped portion only. days_to_resolution reflects closure in the system, which is an administrative act, not necessarily the date the work was done. Duplicate reporting exists and is flagged in the source but not fully deduplicated.

6. Equity: who waits, and where

The central analysis joins tract-level median response times to ACS demographics and to 1930s HOLC grades. A tract is included once it has at least 20 resolved actionable requests; tracts are weighted by resolved volume in the regression so that thin tracts cannot drive the result.

6.1 Response time by historical HOLC grade

HOLC gradeTractsMedian of tract medians (days) % non-whiteMedian household income
A66.3024.7%$134,707
B666.1866.4%$75,504
C4115.9569.6%$74,401
D2965.5373.0%$81,237
Finding 1 (null result). The expected redlining gradient does not appear in response time. Grade D tracts have a median tract response time of 5.53 days against 6.3 days for grade A (ratio 0.879×); the one-sided test for "D is slower" returns p = 0.83, so the hypothesis is not supported. Two caveats keep this honest in both directions: grade A contains only 6 tracts, and the HOLC maps cover roughly three-quarters of the city. What does hold is that grade D tracts are far less white today (73.0% non-white against 24.7% in grade A), and racial composition is the variable most associated with response time — though on this sample that association is marginal, not significant (Finding 2).

6.2 Income, racial composition and response time

Finding 2. A weighted least-squares regression of tract median response time on median income and racial composition (weighted by resolved request count, n = 776 tracts) gives a coefficient of 0.0095 days per percentage point of non-white population (p = 0.064) and -0.1436 days per additional $10,000 of median household income (p = 1e-06). Both run in the expected direction — more non-white and lower-income tracts wait longer — and the income term is the stronger of the two. These are correlates, not mechanisms: neither staffing, routing, nor intake channel is observed here. This regression necessarily drops the tracts whose ACS income estimate is unavailable, which are disproportionately disadvantaged.

6.3 Spatial autocorrelation

If slow service were scattered randomly, it would suggest idiosyncratic local problems. If it clusters, it suggests a systemic geographic pattern. Moran's I with 999 permutations tests this without assuming a distribution.

Finding 3. Tract median response times are spatially clustered: Moran's I = 0.5869 (permutation p = 0.0010, z = 29.65, 789 tracts). Local Moran (LISA) identifies 118 tracts in significant high–high "slow" clusters — neighbouring slow tracts are slow together, so the pattern is systemic rather than a set of unrelated local problems. This spatial result is the most robust equity finding in the analysis; see Finding 1 for why the 1930s grade comparison does not reproduce it.

6.4 Consistency with the City's own hardship measure

  • Across 77 community areas with at least 50 resolved requests, the city's own hardship index correlates with median resolution time at Spearman ρ = +0.154 (p = 1.82e-01). More deprived areas wait longer.

7. Forecasting demand

Monthly request volume is forecast with two approaches against two baselines: seasonal naive (the same month one year earlier) and the in-sample mean. Validation is a 12-month hold-out, backed by a rolling-origin backtest over 24 months, and the hold-out deliberately coincides with the period pulled at full row-level detail.

Finding 4. The best-performing model on the hold-out was SARIMAX + weather. Seasonal naive is a genuinely strong baseline on this series because the summer peak dominates the variance — reporting a model that fails to beat it would be self-deception, so it is reported prominently.
Forecasting caveats. The window contains an exogenous structural break (2020), so a model validated only inside that period is scoring a regime that may not repeat. Intake policy changes — a new app, a changed call flow — would invalidate the seasonal structure entirely. These forecasts describe expected call volume under normal conditions; they are not service-level commitments.

8. Anomaly detection

Weekly volume is screened with Isolation Forest (5% contamination, 500 trees) on seasonal-normalised features, so the model flags weeks that differ from their own historic norm rather than weeks that are merely busy. A transparent seasonal rule is computed alongside it as a sanity benchmark.

Finding 5. The Isolation Forest flagged 16 weeks as anomalous. The model catches weeks that a simple volume threshold misses — weeks with an abnormal severity mix or an abnormal resolution time at normal volume. Each flag is a week for a human to check against the weather record and the intake log; a flag is not a conclusion.
Anomaly caveats. Contamination is chosen, not discovered; the ranking is the trustworthy output and the count is a convenience. Multi-week events produce consecutive flags that are one incident, not several.

9. Recommendations

For city policymakers

  1. Report response time in two tiers. Publish median resolution time for actionable service requests separately from administrative filings. The current single figure is dominated by one-minute closures and understates real service times by a factor of roughly 497,154. This is a reporting change, not a service change, and it is the cheapest credibility win available.
  2. Audit the slow clusters, not the slow complaints. The significant high–high clusters identified in Figure 7 give a concrete, bounded list of 118 census tracts — and the community areas behind them — where a service audit would be most informative. Start there rather than citywide.
  3. Set a severity-differentiated service standard. A 30-day closure on a tree trim and on a flooded basement are not the same outcome. The severity bands provide a ready-made basis for tiered targets, and the pipeline already reports the weighted measure needed to monitor them.
  4. Use the seasonal peak for capacity, not the annual average. Capacity planned on mean annual volume is structurally short in summer.
  5. Publish tract-level response metrics as a standing dataset. The pipeline in this repository regenerates them end to end; a quarterly publication would make the equity conversation evidence-based instead of anecdotal.

For analysts reusing this work

  1. Filter on is_actionable before computing any timing statistic. The single most consequential step in this analysis was noticing the one-minute closures.
  2. Normalise by tract population or request volume before comparing areas, and weight regressions by resolved volume.
  3. Treat the 20% sample and the full-detail months as distinct scopes, and validate the sample against exact counts whenever the API is reachable.
  4. Prefer median and P90 over mean for resolution time. The distribution is extremely right-skewed.

10. Reproducing this analysis

conda create -n chicago311 -c conda-forge python=3.12 \
    duckdb lightgbm geopandas pyarrow jupyter statsmodels \
    scikit-learn matplotlib seaborn scipy
conda activate chicago311
pip install -r requirements.txt

python src/fetch.py --all          # collect all upstream sources
python src/etl.py                  # build the DuckDB warehouse + quality report
python src/generate_notebooks.py   # build and execute the 4 notebooks
python src/build_hyper.py          # Tableau .hyper extract + tract GeoJSON
python src/build_powerbi.py        # Power BI PBIP project
python src/build_html_dashboard.py # self-contained HTML dashboard
python src/build_report.py         # this report

Runtime depends on the collection step, which downloads roughly 21M rows of source data (~5.8 GB) from a rate-limited public API. Everything downstream of collection runs in minutes. All random processes are seeded; all command-line entry points are idempotent.

Statement of limitations. (1) The analysis is observational and the demographic associations are correlates, not causes. (2) Neither crew routing, departmental budgets, staffing nor intake channel are observed, so no mechanism is identified. (3) Closure time records an administrative act, not the date work was completed. (4) HOLC grades cover only the mapped portion of the city. (5) The redlining overlay is descriptive historical context; no causal claim is made about the 1930s maps. (6) One-third of the earliest months are a 20% sample, validated against exact counts but not identical to them.
All statistics in this report were produced by the pipeline in this repository and read programmatically from data/processed/findings.json and the DuckDB warehouse. No figure in the text was transcribed by hand.
